# The SystemVerilog Testbench Language {#sec-ch05}

*Two-state for what the testbench computes; four-state for what it observes.*

::: {.callout-note title="Learning objectives"}
After this chapter you can choose two-state or four-state for a testbench variable and say what each hides; pick the right aggregate for a job and name its cost; declare a protocol as a packed struct and an enum; connect a testbench to a design through an interface and hold it through a virtual interface; explain what a class handle is, what `new` does, and when an object dies; read the lifetime of a variable off where it is declared; sample and drive at a clock edge through a clocking block; and state, for every one of those constructs, which of this book's two open simulators runs it.
:::

## A reset that never happened

A testbench declared its reset line as `bit rst_n`, drove it low, released it, and went on to run a thousand cycles against a design that had never been reset. Nothing failed. The design's registers started at zero, because that is where a two-state simulator starts everything; zero was a legal value for each of them; and the checks that followed were written against a model that also started at zero. The bug surfaced on silicon, where registers do not start anywhere in particular.

The mechanism is in the declaration. A `bit` starts at zero, and zero is the active level of an active-low reset. When the testbench then assigns zero to it there is no transition, so there is no `negedge rst_n` event, so the asynchronous reset block in the design never runs. The two-state simulator has no way to say that anything is wrong, because nothing in its world is: a variable held a value, and then held it again. Sutherland and Mills cataloged this as the first of four ways a two-state model hides a bug — one of them in the testbench, three in the design — and every one of the four reduces to the same sentence: the model started at zero, and zero was legal [@sutherland2006gotchas].

This chapter is about the language a testbench is written in, and it opens with that bug because the language's first decision is the one that caused it. Everything else here — aggregates, structs, interfaces, classes, clocking blocks — is a construct that either runs on the tools this book uses or does not, and the chapter ends by measuring which.

## Two kinds of value {#sec-ch05-types}

SystemVerilog has two value sets. A four-state variable holds 0, 1, X or Z; a two-state variable holds 0 or 1. `logic`, `reg`, `integer` and `wire` are four-state; `bit`, `byte`, `shortint`, `int` and `longint` are two-state, and the last four are 8, 16, 32 and 64 bits wide and signed. `logic` and `bit` take the width you give them and are unsigned unless you say otherwise [@ieee1800-2023].

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
A **two-state** variable cannot hold an unknown. Assigning X to it stores 0 [@sutherland2006gotchas]. A **four-state** variable can hold an unknown, and every operator in @sec-ch04-fourstate that propagates X propagates it through a four-state variable and stops at a two-state one.
:::

The rule for the testbench is the inverse of the rule for the design. Sutherland and Mills argue that RTL should avoid two-state types altogether, because they can hide design problems and lead to a mismatch between simulation and synthesis — the 2006 catalog is where the hidden problems are shown one by one, the forgotten reset and the unconnected input among them [@sutherland2006gotchas] — and they note in passing that verification code is different: randomly generated test values should be declared two-state, with the reasoning deferred to Sutherland's paper on X [@sutherlandmills2013synth]. That paper's guideline is the one this chapter adopts: variables that will or might take randomly generated values are declared two-state, the iterator of a `for` loop is an `int`, and two-state types are used for those and for nothing else [@sutherland2013x]. This chapter goes further than that guideline, and says so: it puts everything the testbench *computes* in two-state, not only the random stimulus, because a counter, an expected value or a scoreboard entry is a value the testbench made, an X in one of them is a bug in the testbench rather than a finding about the design, and a two-state declaration is what keeps such an X from being carried silently into a comparison. One fact from the 2007 gotchas paper belongs beside it, because it is easy to get backwards: unconstrained randomization ranges over every value of the variable's type, so a signed type yields negative stimulus and a stimulus variable's declared type is also its distribution — and that paper's own advice for such variables is the four-state `logic`, for the sign rather than the value set, which this chapter departs from in favor of the guideline above [@sutherland2007gotchas]. The testbench rule is: Two-state for what the testbench *computes* — stimulus, counters, expected values, scoreboards — because those values are the testbench's own and an X among them is a testbench bug. Four-state for what the testbench *observes* — anything sampled from the design — because an X coming out of the design is a finding, and a two-state variable would convert it to a legal zero before any check could see it.

That is a different statement from the one @sec-ch04-fourstate makes. That section is about what the *simulator* can represent; this is about what the *declaration* at the boundary lets through. A four-state simulator with a two-state variable at the boundary loses the unknown at the boundary.

### What a two-state variable cannot see

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall"}
The four two-state traps in the 2006 catalog are one trap: a two-state variable starts at zero, and zero is a legal value. A reset declared `bit` never produces the edge that asserts it. A state machine whose reset state is its enum's first value gets, at reset, a value it already holds: no transition, so nothing downstream that waits on the state ever wakes, and the model stays put with the clock running. An input nobody connected reads as zero rather than as X. An out-of-bounds array read returns zero rather than X. In each case the four-state model behaves differently — the reset assignment is a transition, the unconnected input is an X that propagates, the bad read is an X — and the difference is what makes the bug visible [@sutherland2006gotchas].
:::

The opening bug is the first of those, and it is reproducible on both of this book's simulators. The design is a register with an asynchronous active-low reset whose reset value is deliberately not zero, so that a reset that never happens is visible:

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/twostate-reset/dut_reg.sv"}
```

Three testbenches drive it. The first declares the reset `bit` and does what the story's testbench did; the second declares it `logic`; the third manufactures an edge. The reset is pulsed *before* the first clock edge in each, because the reset is asynchronous and a clock edge during the pulse would load the register through the level test in the block whatever the declaration — the point is what the `negedge` event does on its own.

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/twostate-reset/tb_bit.sv"}
```

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/twostate-reset/tb_logic.sv"}
```

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/twostate-reset/tb_fixed.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/twostate-reset/run_both.sh"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/twostate-reset/run.out"}
```

Read the six lines as three pairs. With `bit`, neither simulator sees an edge, and the four-state one shows what that leaves behind: the register is `xx`, unknown, because nothing ever wrote it. With `logic`, the four-state simulator starts the variable at X, so the write of 0 is an X-to-0 transition, which is a `negedge`, and the reset runs; the two-state simulator starts `logic` at zero too — the declaration changed nothing it could see — and the register stays unwritten, reading as zero. Only the third testbench resets on both, and its fix is not the one the literature prints. The 2006 paper's two-line fix drives the line inactive with a blocking assignment and then active with a non-blocking one, so that the two writes land in different regions of one timestep and the simulator sees 1 then 0 [@sutherland2006gotchas]. The event-driven simulator does see that. The statically scheduled one compares values between evaluations (@sec-ch04-real), and across the timestep the line went from 0 to 0. An edge one time unit later is an edge both tools see, and that is the version the listing uses. Verilator documents an option, `--x-initial-edge`, for code that relies on an X-to-0 transition triggering an edge [@verilator-languages]; under the timing mode this book's build uses, the 5.030 release aborts at run time with it on every testbench in this listing, so the conclusion above stands with the flags the book runs.

::: {.callout-tip title="In Practice"}
Declare the reset `logic`, drive it inactive first, and put a delay between inactive and active. Then the design resets on any simulator, the first clock edge is not needed to do the reset's job, and a four-state simulator can still show you a register nobody wrote.
:::

## Aggregates: arrays, queues, associative arrays {#sec-ch05-aggregates}

Four containers, and two questions choose between them: what is the index, and is the size known when the code is written? A fixed array answers both up front. A dynamic array has an integer index and a size decided at run time. A queue is a dynamic array that grows and shrinks at either end and can be inserted into in the middle. An associative array is indexed by a key of any type — an address, a string, a struct — and holds only the entries that were written [@ieee1800-2023].

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/aggregates/tb_aggregates.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/aggregates/run.out"}
```

The queue is the scoreboard's natural shape: transactions go in at the back in the order they were sent and come off the front in the order they should arrive, and `q[$]` is always the last one. The associative array is the memory model's natural shape: a design with a 32-bit address space touches a few hundred addresses in a test, and an associative array keyed by address stores those and nothing else. OpenTitan's shared memory model is exactly that, an associative array of bytes keyed by address, and the base scoreboard of its comportable-IP library holds one per memory [@opentitan-mem-model; @opentitan-cip-scoreboard].

::: {.callout-tip title="In Practice"}
Say what each operation costs in shape, not in numbers. Pushing and popping at a queue's ends touches one element; inserting in the middle has, by the queue's own definition of order, to renumber everything after the insertion point. An associative array's lookup is a search keyed on the index and its iteration with `first`/`next` visits entries in key order. No public source measures any of this for a particular simulator, so this book does not print a figure; a scoreboard that is slow is measured on the tool that runs it, not predicted.
:::

Two habits keep the two-state rule from being broken by an aggregate. Declare a scoreboard's *expected* values two-state, because the testbench computed them; declare what was *sampled* four-state, because the design produced it. And when an associative array's `first` and `next` are used as conditions, compare their `int` result to zero explicitly — the listing does — because a lint pass under the book's flags otherwise reports the truncation, and it is right to.

## Naming things: `struct`, `union`, `enum`, `typedef`, `string` {#sec-ch05-structs}

A packed struct is a vector with named fields. The same bits can be read by name or as a whole, and assigning the whole changes the fields. That makes it the right declaration for a bus transaction: the wire format is the vector, the fields are what the protocol calls them, and a testbench never has to know which bits the tag lives in. A packed union of two packed layouts is an honest reinterpretation of one set of bits — a word that is sometimes a header and sometimes payload — and an unpacked one is a cast wearing a type's name. An enum is a type with a closed set of names, and the closure is what makes it useful and where it leaks [@ieee1800-2023].

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/structs-enums/tb_structs.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/structs-enums/run.out"}
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall"}
The enum hole. `$cast` and `.next()` refuse a value outside the enum's set, and `$cast` says so by returning zero. A static cast — `state_t'(3)` — forces the value in, and the variable then holds a state with no name: `.name()` returns the empty string and every `case` on it falls through. A design's state register can get there through a two-state reset that never happened (@sec-ch05-types), and a testbench that compares states by name will never notice [@sutherland2006gotchas].
:::

OpenTitan's TileLink package is the shape to copy: each direction of the bus is a packed struct, the structs are typed and exported from one package [@opentitan-tlul-pkg], and the TileLink agent's interface carries them as they are, so its monitor and drivers speak in field names rather than bit ranges [@opentitan-tl-if].

## Interfaces {#sec-ch05-interfaces}

An interface is a named bundle of signals with its own ports and its own code. A modport is a view of the bundle: a list of which of its signals a module connected through that view may drive and which it may only read. The same wire is an output on the testbench's view and an input on the design's, and a module that drives through the wrong view fails to compile [@ieee1800-2023].

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/interface-vif/bus_if.sv"}
```

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/interface-vif/sink.sv"}
```

The two lowRISC style guides differ about interfaces, on the record, and the difference is the lesson. The RTL guide considers interfaces problematic and discourages their use unless a rule says otherwise; the DV guide tells you to use clocking blocks inside an interface to sample and drive a synchronous design interface [@lowrisc-verilog-style; @lowrisc-dv-style]. Sutherland and Mills draw the distinction that reconciles them: an interface's purpose is to bundle signals that are related — a bus, not every port of a module — and verification is the exception, where an interface between testbench and design may bundle signals that are not functionally related at all [@sutherlandmills2013synth]. The reason the exception holds is this chapter's, not theirs: a design bundles signals that belong together electrically; a testbench bundles signals that belong together *procedurally* — everything one driver touches — and an interface is the only unit of the design hierarchy that can be handed to a class.

That handing is the virtual interface. A class cannot instantiate an interface, because a class is not part of the design hierarchy; it can hold a *variable* whose value is a handle to an interface instance, and drive the wires through the handle. The word to keep is variable. A virtual interface starts null like every other variable and is typed like every other variable, and every virtual-interface failure a testbench has is a variable's failure: the null dereference when it is used before it is set, the compile error at the assignment when the class's declared parameters do not match the instance it is given, and the silent nothing when it is set to the wrong instance [@sutherland2007gotchas; @rich2012missinglink].

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/interface-vif/tb_vif.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/interface-vif/run.out"}
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall"}
Three virtual-interface failures, one cause. A handle used before it is set; a handle whose parameters do not match the instance; a handle set to the wrong instance. Each is "it is a variable" seen from a different side, and the defense is the same for all three: check for null before the first drive, as the listing's driver does, and fail loudly rather than drive nothing. OpenTitan's TileLink agent sets its virtual interface through a configuration database and fatal-errors on a missing one, which is that check written once for every test that uses the agent [@opentitan-tl-if]. How the handle gets set — the connection strategy — is the subject of the chapter on connecting testbench and design, later in Part II.
:::

## Classes: handles and objects {#sec-ch05-classes}

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
A **class** is a type with data members and methods. An **object** is an instance of one, created by `new`. A **handle** is a variable that names an object; it is what a class-typed variable holds, and it starts `null`. Assigning one handle to another makes two names for one object [@ieee1800-2023].
:::

Everything that goes wrong with classes in a testbench goes wrong at the line between the handle and the object, so the listing draws it in four steps: a handle before `new` is null; `b = a` is an alias, and a write through `b` is visible through `a`; a copy is a new object with the same values, which only a method that calls `new` can make; and setting a handle to null does nothing to the object if another handle still names it.

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/class-handles/tb_handles.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/class-handles/run.out"}
```

The static member is the other line worth drawing. `made` belongs to the class, not to any object: every object sees the same one, and it is reached through the class scope operator, `packet::made`, without an object at all. That is where a transaction's sequence number lives, and it is also where a bug lives when a designer meant one counter per object and got one per class.

When does an object die? The standard promises that an object no one can reach is reclaimed, and promises nothing about when, and provides no destructor to run at that moment [@ieee1800-2023]. What a tool does with that latitude is its own business, and one of this book's tools documents its choice: Verilator counts references, and the issue that proposed a tracing collector for it records that a UVM component tree, whose parents hold their children and whose children hold their parents, forms cycles that reference counting never frees [@verilator-issue-4651]. A testbench that creates and drops objects in a loop should know which of those it is running on.

What this chapter does *not* teach is the second half of the class system. Inheritance, virtual methods, polymorphism and the patterns built on them are the next chapter's subject, and the line is drawn where the standard text draws it: Spear and Tumbush have a chapter titled "Basic OOP" and, a hundred pages apart, one titled "Advanced OOP and Testbench Guidelines", and this chapter and the next observe the same split [@spear2012svfv]. `$cast` appears here only as the enum check it is; what it does across a class hierarchy waits for the hierarchy.

## Automatic and static; passing by reference {#sec-ch05-lifetime}

A variable's lifetime is readable off where it is declared. A task or function in a module or a package is static: there is one copy of each of its variables, shared by every call, and two calls in flight at once overwrite each other. Declared `automatic`, each call gets its own. A class method is automatic by default. A `ref` argument — a reference into the caller's variable rather than a copy of it — is legal only on an automatic subroutine [@ieee1800-2023]. That rule is the standard's, and the reason behind it is this chapter's reading: a static subroutine has nowhere safe to keep the reference between calls. And neither of this book's tools enforces it — one accepts `ref` on a static task without a warning, the other rejects `ref` altogether.

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/lifetime/tb_lifetime.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/lifetime/run.out"}
```

The static task's two callers corrupt each other on one simulator and happen not to on the other, and that is the trap in one output: the corruption depends on how the two calls interleave, which the language does not fix and each tool decides for itself. A testbench with a static task that has been correct for a year on one simulator can become wrong on another, or when a delay changes. The `ref` argument is a separate listing, because one of the two tools does not accept `ref` at all:

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/ref-argument/tb_ref.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/ref-argument/run.out"}
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall"}
Two lifetime bugs from the 2007 catalog, one a static where an automatic was meant and one a copy where a reference was. A watchdog task declared in a program and started twice shares one timer between the two starts. A handle assigned inside an `input` argument updates the subroutine's copy of the handle and not the caller's, so a function that builds two objects and hands them back through its arguments hands back nothing [@sutherland2007gotchas]. Read the declaration before reading the body.
:::

## Clocking blocks: the testbench's clock edge {#sec-ch05-clocking}

A clocking block names a clock and says, for each signal it lists, when the testbench reads it and when the testbench's writes land. `input #1step` reads the value from just before the edge; `output #0` writes just after it. @sec-ch04-boundary explained why that matters: a testbench that samples in the same region the design updates in is racing it, and a clocking block moves the testbench's reads and writes out of that region by construction [@ieee1800-2023; @cummingssalz2007events].

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/clocking/tb_clocking.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/clocking/run.out"}
```

Each line reads the value the design had settled before this edge and drives what the design will see at the next one, and the design's own increment shows up one line later, where it should. A `program` block is the other construct the standard offers for the same purpose: code inside one runs in the Reactive region set, after the design's regions in every timestep (@sec-ch04-regions). This book's testbenches are modules with clocking blocks rather than programs. Both of this book's simulators run a `program` block, as the table below shows, so the choice is not a tool's; it follows the lowRISC DV style guide, whose first rule is not to use the `program` construct at all, and the same guide's rule that clocking blocks in an interface are what a testbench samples and drives through [@lowrisc-dv-style].

## What runs where {#sec-ch05-tools}

Every listing in this chapter runs — the two-simulator ones under both tools, and the rest under Verilator, each Makefile naming the construct Icarus refuses, which the table below shows for interface ports, virtual interfaces, clocking blocks, associative arrays, the class scope operator and `$cast` on an enum, and which the Makefiles show for a chained enum method and `ref`. The reason each runs where it does is a fact about the tool rather than the language. The table records that fact for every construct the chapter teaches. Each row is one probe, run under Verilator with the flags this book's build uses and under Icarus with `-g2012`, and a row says *runs* only if the probe compiled, ran and printed the values it expected — a probe that prints the wrong value is recorded as wrong, not as running.

{{< include /examples/ch05-testbench-language/support-matrix/matrix.md >}}

The table is regenerated from the probes on every build, by the example that follows, so it cannot say something the tools have stopped doing:

```{.python include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/support-matrix/matrix.py"}
```

Three things in it decide the shape of this chapter and the next two.

The first is the column of *no build* under Icarus for interfaces as module ports, virtual interfaces, parameterized classes, clocking blocks and associative arrays. Each is a tracked gap: the interface-port issue has been open since 2021 and its fix was merged two and a half months after the release this book measures [@icarus-issue-464; @icarus-pr-1348; @icarus-release-13]; the clocking-block, virtual-interface and parameterized-class issues have been open since 2021, 2017 and 2019 [@icarus-issue-465; @icarus-issue-166; @icarus-issue-291]; associative arrays are an issue open since 2022 [@icarus-issue-792]. So this chapter's interface, clocking and worked examples run under Verilator, and say so in their Makefiles.

The second is the cells that say *wrong*, because a tool that refuses a construct is safe and a tool that runs it and prints the wrong answer is not. Four say it; two are for a missing solver and are discussed below, and two are for a language construct. Verilator stores zero for a four-state constant, which is its documented two-state model [@verilator-languages] and is why the four-state half of @sec-ch05-types has to be read on the Icarus lines of its output. And Icarus 13.0 calls a virtual method through a base-class handle and runs the *base* class's body, with no warning: an inheritance example on it compiles, runs and prints the wrong output. That is the first thing the next chapter has to say, and it is why the chapter's inheritance row is split into a call on the derived handle, which both tools get right, and a call through the base handle, which one does not.

The third is the bottom of the table. Randomization with constraints prints the wrong answer on Verilator and does not compile on Icarus, and the reason is not a language gap: Verilator delegates constraint solving to an external solver, added in its 5.026 release, and with none installed `randomize()` returns without solving [@verilator-changes]. Constrained-random stimulus is its own chapter in Part II, and that chapter begins by installing a solver.

::: {.callout-tip title="In Practice"}
A parser is not a simulator, and for a class of checks that is the point. slang accepts the whole language, including everything in the table's *no build* cells, and can elaborate a testbench that neither simulator here will run [@slang-docs]. A lint pass through it catches the modport driven from the wrong side and the parameter mismatch on a virtual interface before either simulator is asked. The Python track this book runs alongside, cocotb, sidesteps the whole table: its testbench is Python, the design is whatever the simulator accepts, and the constructs above never reach the simulator at all [@cocotb-docs].
:::

## Worked example: one transaction, from the design's port to the scoreboard {#sec-ch05-example}

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example"}
The FIFO of @sec-ch01, driven and checked by a testbench built from everything in this chapter: a packed struct as the wire format, a class with a static member as the transaction, a queue of handles as the scoreboard, an interface holding a clocking block as the boundary, and two classes reaching it through virtual interfaces. Six packets go in and six come out, in order.
:::

The interface bundles the FIFO's ports and puts the clocking block beside them, so the design sees wires and the testbench sees settled values:

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/packet-fifo/fifo_if.sv"}
```

The transaction is a class around a packed struct. The struct is what the FIFO stores, bit for bit; the class is what the testbench keeps — an identity, a comparison, a way to print itself:

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/packet-fifo/packet.sv"}
```

The producer pushes each packet's handle onto the scoreboard before driving its word in; the consumer reads a word out and pops the handle that should match. Both hold the same scoreboard and the same interface through handles, so there is exactly one of each:

```{.systemverilog include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/packet-fifo/tb_packet_fifo.sv"}
```

```{.text include="examples/ch05-testbench-language/packet-fifo/run.out"}
```

Two things in that listing are choices the support table forced, and both are worth seeing. The interface has no modport carrying the clocking block, because a `modport (clocking cb)` is one of the constructs the default simulator refuses; the classes hold the whole interface and reach `cb` through it. And the classes are declared at file scope rather than inside the testbench module, because the default simulator fails with an internal error on a class declared inside a module that refers to any of the module's own variables — a queue, an `int`, a task alike — which is why the scoreboard became a class of its own, and the design is better for it.

::: {.callout-important title="Future Directions"}
A type system this strict is exactly what a program can check, and the checks are cheap once a parser that accepts the whole language exists. The constructs a simulator does not run are the ones an agent's tools must refuse rather than emit: a testbench generator that produces a `modport (clocking)` for a flow that runs on Verilator has produced a compile error, and the table above is the specification of which constructs that is. The tool-layer appendix develops the idea; here the point is that the table is data, and a program can read it before a person has to.
:::

## Summary

- A two-state variable converts an unknown to a legal zero. Two-state for what the testbench computes; four-state for what it observes.
- A reset declared `bit` never produces the edge that asserts it; and the published two-line fix works on the event-driven simulator only. An edge across time works on both.
- Fixed, dynamic, queue, associative: choose by what the index is and whether the size is known. The queue is a scoreboard's shape; the associative array is a memory model's.
- A packed struct is a vector with named fields, and the right declaration for a bus transaction. An enum is closed for `$cast` and `.next()` and open for a static cast.
- An interface bundles what one driver touches; a modport says who may drive what; a virtual interface is a variable, so it starts null and must be checked.
- A handle names an object; `=` copies the name, not the object; a static member belongs to the class; an unreachable object is reclaimed at no promised time.
- Lifetime is readable off the declaration: module and package subroutines are static, class methods automatic, and `ref` needs automatic.
- A clocking block moves the testbench's reads and writes out of the design's regions by construction.
- Of the constructs this chapter teaches, thirteen run on both open simulators and fourteen on exactly one; two run and print the wrong answer in silence, a four-state constant on one tool and a virtual method on the other. The table is measured, not asserted.

## Exercises

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise"}
1. Declare the same counter `bit` and `logic`, drive it from an unreset source, and show what each prints on both simulators.
2. Replace the worked example's queue scoreboard with an associative array keyed by sequence number. Say what got cheaper and what got harder.
3. Write a packed struct for the FIFO's write transaction and a `$cast`-guarded enum for its state. Make the static cast fail, and find a `case` statement that falls through because of it.
4. Add a second modport to the worked example's interface and connect a second testbench through a virtual interface. Set the handle to null and read the error each simulator gives.
5. The lifetime listing's static task corrupts on the event-driven simulator and not on the statically scheduled one. Change the delays until it corrupts on the second as well, or show that no delay does, and explain why the `automatic` version cannot corrupt on either.
6. Add a row to the support table for a construct not in it, with the probe that measured it, and say which of the three chapters that construct belongs to.
:::

## Further reading

Sutherland's DVCon 2013 paper on X states the two-state guideline this chapter starts from [@sutherland2013x]; Sutherland and Mills' SNUG 2013 paper gives the RTL-side rule and the distinction between an interface that bundles related signals and one that bundles a testbench's [@sutherlandmills2013synth]. The two "gotchas" papers, by Sutherland and Mills and then with Chris Spear on the second, catalog the traps this chapter draws on, each with its fix [@sutherland2006gotchas; @sutherland2007gotchas]. Spear and Tumbush's book is the standard text for the class system, and its chapter boundary is the one this chapter and the next observe [@spear2012svfv]. Rich's DVCon paper on connecting a testbench to a design is the primary account of virtual interfaces and their alternatives [@rich2012missinglink]. The lowRISC DV style guide is a public, production-grade statement of how the constructs here are used together [@lowrisc-dv-style]. For what the two open simulators implement, Verilator's language page is the source; Icarus documents its gaps through its diagnostics and its issue tracker rather than a page, and the table above is the measurement for both [@verilator-languages; @icarus-issue-464; @icarus-issue-792].
